title: Om jai jagadish hare
hookLine: Gajendra calls on Hari from the crocodile's grip; the arti song sings that rescue
carry: hari, the one who takes the trouble away
last: NARADA'S MONKEY FACE — BURN THE EGO LIKE CAMPHOR.

lines: A LAKE, A HERD, A CROCODILE.
cards: A lake high on a mountain, thick with lotuses. The king of the elephants, Gajendra, wades in with his whole herd to bathe. Then something grabs his leg.
A crocodile, and it won't let go. He pulls toward the shore; it pulls toward the deep. His family try to drag him out and can't.
In the telling, the struggle goes on for years, and slowly the strongest animal on the mountain runs out of strength. His herd can't save him. There's one thing left he can do.

teach.b: This is Gajendra, from the Bhagavata Purana, one of the best-loved stories of Vishnu. Near the end, the elephant lifts a lotus in his trunk and prays. And notice how he prays.
Most of it isn't begging. It's praise: you are the source of everything, the shelter of whoever turns to you. Only then does he ask.

And Vishnu comes at once, cuts the crocodile away with his spinning discus, and pulls the elephant out of the water. Now listen to the song that's sung while the arti flame circles: Om jai jagadish hare. Jai, victory.

teach.h: HARI: THE ONE WHO TAKES AWAY.
teach.b: Hare calls on Hari, a name of Vishnu that tradition explains as the one who takes away: takes away what has hold of you. The next lines say it plainly: the troubles of your devotees, you take away in a moment.
That's Gajendra's story in one line.

teach.h: A HINDI SONG, AN OLD TEACHING.
teach.b: The song itself isn't ancient. It's usually credited to Shardha Ram Phillauri, a Punjabi writer of the eighteen-hundreds, and it's in Hindi, so anyone could understand it. But what it teaches is old.
This is bhakti, loving devotion. Gajendra was the strongest one on the mountain, and strength ran out.
What he had left was a name to call. Many teachers read the crocodile as whatever has hold of you that you can't pull free from alone.
So the song starts with praise, jai, then remembers that people are hurting, and trusts Hari to come quickly.

how: In many Hindu homes and temples, especially in North India and the diaspora, Om jai jagadish hare is sung while the arti lamp is circled at the end of puja, with a bell ringing and everyone joining in.

o: a Hindi word that means victory or glory
the elephant king caught in the lake
a name of Vishnu: the one who takes away

games.q: the elephant and the song — tap the pairs.
p: the elephant king caught in the lake
the grip he can't pull free from

s: Gajendra's prayer is mostly a list of requests
most of it is praise of the lord who shelters everyone; only then does he ask.
the arti song says Hari takes away his devotees' troubles
the same thing Vishnu does for Gajendra in the lake, at once.
Om jai jagadish hare is thousands of years old
it's usually credited to Shardha Ram Phillauri, a Punjabi writer of the nineteenth century. its teaching is much older.

games.q: you're Gajendra. your herd has tried everything, your strength is gone, and the crocodile still has your leg. what does the story have you do?
o: keep pulling alone until you win.
lift a lotus and call on the lord, praising him first.
make a deal with the crocodile.
games.why: the elephant prays, mostly in praise, and Vishnu comes at once. that's bhakti: when strength runs out, you call on Hari, the one who takes troubles away.

practice: Slowly, speak it, sing it or just listen inside: Om jai jagadish hare, swami jai jagadish hare. Once more, a little slower; if you'd like, let a flame or your open hand circle with the tune.

Then name, silently, one thing that has hold of you right now, and lift it up the way the elephant lifted his lotus. If you don't pray, simply listen to the words and the tune, and let the sound settle.

wordCard.voice: Hari, a name of Vishnu, the one who takes away: the name Gajendra called from the lake, and the one the arti song calls, Om jai jagadish hare. Today's word.

orig.note: Hindi: Om, victory to the lord of the world, O Hari.

carryVoice: Your line: Hari, the one who takes the trouble away. The elephant called, and help came at once. Day one hundred twenty, done.
